claim: Overlapping genes (OLGs) are common in viruses and have been associated with pandemics but are still widely overlooked.
source: Overlapping genes (OLGs) are common in viruses and have been associated with pandemics but are still widely overlooked.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about OLGs in viruses and their association with pandemics.

claim: ORF3d is a novel OLG in SARS-CoV-2 that is also present in Guangxi pangolin-CoVs but not other closely related pangolin-CoVs or bat-CoVs.
source: We identify and characterize ORF3d, a novel OLG in SARS-CoV-2 that is also present in Guangxi pangolin-CoVs but not other closely related pangolin-CoVs or bat-CoVs.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing the presence of ORF3d in SARS-CoV-2 and Guangxi pangolin-CoVs through sequence analysis and alignment.

claim: ORF3d has been independently identified and shown to elicit a strong antibody response in COVID-19 patients.
source: ORF3d has been independently identified and shown to elicit a strong antibody response in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This statement references independent work by other researchers (Hachim et al., 2020) showing antibody responses to ORF3d.

claim: ORF3d has been misclassified as the unrelated gene ORF3b, leading to confusion.
source: However, it has been misclassified as the unrelated gene ORF3b, leading to confusion.
evidence: The manuscript provides evidence through sequence alignment and genomic position analysis showing that ORF3d and ORF3b are distinct genes.

claim: Overlapping genes compress genomic information and allow genetic innovation via overprinting.
source: Such 'genes within genes' compress genomic information and allow genetic innovation via overprinting (Keese and Gibbs, 1992), particularly as frameshifted sequences preserve certain physicochemical properties of proteins (Bartonek et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on the properties of overlapping genes.

claim: OLGs entail the cost that a single mutation may alter two proteins, constraining evolution of the pre-existing open reading frame.
source: However, OLGs also entail the cost that a single mutation may alter two proteins, constraining evolution of the pre-existing open reading frame (ORF) and complicating sequence analysis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the evolutionary constraints imposed by overlapping genes.

claim: Genome annotation methods typically miss OLGs, instead favoring one ORF per genomic region.
source: Unfortunately, genome annotation methods typically miss OLGs, instead favoring one ORF per genomic region (Warren et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Warren et al., 2010 discussing limitations of annotation methods.

claim: OLGs are known entities but remain inconsistently reported in viruses of the species Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus.
source: OLGs are known entities but remain inconsistently reported in viruses of the species Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus (subgenus Sarbecovirus; genus Betacoronavirus; Coronaviridae Study Group of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by examples of inconsistent annotation in reference genomes and studies.

claim: Annotations of ORF9b and ORF9c are absent or conflicting in SARS-CoV-2 reference genome Wuhan-Hu-1 and genomic studies.
source: For example, annotations of ORF9b and ORF9c are absent or conflicting in SARS-CoV-2 reference genome Wuhan-Hu-1 (NCBI: NC_045512.2) and genomic studies (e.g. Chan et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020b), and OLGs are often not displayed in genome browsers (e.g. Flynn et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by examination of reference genomes and citations to studies showing inconsistent annotation.

claim: ORF3b is an extensively characterized OLG within ORF3a that is present in other species members including SARS-CoV (SARS-CoV-1).
source: Further, ORF3b, an extensively characterized OLG within ORF3a that is present in other species members including SARS-CoV (SARS-CoV-1) (McBride and Fielding, 2012), has sometimes been annotated in SARS-CoV-2 even though it contains four early STOP codons in this virus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McBride and Fielding, 2012 and sequence analysis showing STOP codons in SARS-CoV-2.

claim: In HIV-1, the novel OLG asp within env is actively expressed in human cells and is associated with the pandemic M group lineage.
source: For example, in human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1), the novel OLG asp within env is actively expressed in human cells (Affram et al., 2019) and is associated with the pandemic M group lineage (Cassan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on HIV-1 OLGs.

claim: ORF3d scored highly (p=0.0104) in the codon permutation method, exceeding the significance of two known OLGs annotated in Uniprot (ORF9b and ORF9c).
source: One unannotated OLG candidate, here named ORF3d, scored highly (p=0.0104), exceeding the significance of two known OLGs annotated in Uniprot (ORF9b and ORF9c, both within N; https://viralzone.expasy.org/8996) (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis using the codon permutation method and comparison to known OLGs.

claim: ORF3d comprises 58 codons (including STOP) near the beginning of ORF3a.
source: ORF3d comprises 58 codons (including STOP) near the beginning of ORF3a (Table 1), making it longer than the known genes ORF7b (44 codons) and ORF10 (39 codons) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison to other genes.

claim: ORF3d was discovered independently by Chan et al., 2020 as 'ORF3b' and Pavesi, 2020 as 'hypothetical protein'.
source: ORF3d was discovered independently by Chan et al., 2020 as 'ORF3b' and Pavesi, 2020 as 'hypothetical protein'.
evidence: This is supported by citations to independent studies that identified the same genomic region.

claim: ORF3d has been conflated with the previously documented ORF3b in multiple studies.
source: Due to this naming ambiguity and its location within ORF3a, ORF3d has subsequently been conflated with the previously documented ORF3b in multiple studies (e.g. Fung et al., 2020; Ge et al., 2020; Gordon et al., 2020; Hachim et al., 2020; Helmy et al., 2020; Yi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies that misidentified ORF3d as ORF3b.

claim: ORF3d is unrelated (not homologous) to ORF3b, as the two genes occupy different genomic positions within ORF3a.
source: Critically, ORF3d is unrelated (i.e. not homologous) to ORF3b, as the two genes occupy different genomic positions within ORF3a: ORF3d ends 39 codons upstream of the genome region homologous to ORF3b, and the ORF3b start site encodes only 23 codons in SARS-CoV-2 due to a premature STOP (Wu et al., 2020a; Table 1, Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and genomic position analysis.

claim: ORF3d and ORF3b occupy different reading frames: codon position 1 of ORF3a overlaps codon position 2 of ORF3d (frame ss12) but codon position 3 of ORF3b (frame ss13).
source: Furthermore, the two genes occupy different reading frames: codon position 1 of ORF3a overlaps codon position 2 of ORF3d (frame ss12) but codon position 3 of ORF3b (frame ss13).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of reading frames.

claim: ORF3d putatively encodes a novel protein not present in previously discovered Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus genomes.
source: Thus, ORF3d putatively encodes a novel protein not present in previously discovered Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus genomes, while the absence of full-length ORF3b in SARS-CoV-2 distinguishes it from SARS-CoV (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis across related coronavirus species.

claim: A consistent peak in ribosome profiling read depth is observed ~12 nt upstream of the start site of ORF3d, the expected ribosomal P-site offset.
source: After trimming reads to their 5′ ends (first nt), we observe a consistent peak in read depth ~12 nt upstream of the start site of ORF3d (Figure 2A), the expected ribosomal P-site offset (Calviello and Ohler, 2017).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ribosome profiling data showing translation initiation.

claim: There is a strong correlation (rS = 0.89, p=0.0004) between protein expression as estimated from mass spectrometry and the ribosome profiling read depth observed at upstream peaks.
source: However, we do find a strong correlation between protein expression as estimated from MS and the ribosome profiling read depth observed at upstream peaks, with rS = 0.89 (p=0.0004, Spearman's rank) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing mass spectrometry and ribosome profiling data.

claim: The presence and depth of an upstream peak in ribosome profiling is a reliable indicator of gene expression.
source: This suggests that the presence and depth of an upstream peak is a reliable indicator of expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlation between upstream peaks and mass spectrometry data.

claim: N, M, and S are the most highly expressed proteins in SARS-CoV-2, with N constituting ~80% of the total viral protein content.
source: Specifically, results from both proteomic and ribosome profiling approaches confirm that N, M, and S are the most highly expressed proteins, with N constituting ~80% of the total viral protein content.
evidence: This is based on analysis of mass spectrometry and ribosome profiling data.

claim: Sliding windows reveal a peak in the fraction of reads mapping to the reading frame of ORF3d at its hypothesized locus.
source: Sliding windows reveal a peak in the fraction of reads mapping to the reading frame of ORF3d at its hypothesized locus, with this frame's maximum occurring at the center of ORF3d, co-located with a dip in the fraction of reads mapping to the frame of ORF3a (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ribosome profiling data showing frame-specific translation.

claim: These observations suggest that ORF3d is actively translated.
source: These observations suggest that ORF3d is actively translated.
evidence: This is inferred from the ribosome profiling data showing frame-specific peaks.

claim: Gordon et al., 2020 used overexpression experiments to demonstrate that ORF3d can be stably expressed and that it interacts with the mitochondrial protein STOML2.
source: Gordon et al., 2020 used overexpression experiments to demonstrate that ORF3d (referred to as 'ORF3b'; Table 1) can be stably expressed and that it interacts with the mitochondrial protein STOML2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2020 describing experimental results.

claim: ORF3d, ORF8, and N elicit the strongest antibody responses observed in COVID-19 patient sera.
source: Most compellingly, ORF3d, ORF8, and N elicit the strongest antibody responses observed in COVID-19 patient sera, with ORF3d sufficient to accurately diagnose the majority of COVID-19 cases (Hachim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hachim et al., 2020 showing antibody response data.

claim: ORF3d is restricted to SARS-CoV-2 and pangolin-CoV, making cross-reactivity with another coronavirus unlikely.
source: Because ORF3d is restricted to SARS-CoV-2 and pangolin-CoV (see below), this finding is unlikely to be due to cross-reactivity with another coronavirus and provides strong independent evidence of ORF3d translation during infection.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis and inference about antibody specificity.

claim: ORF3d has the lowest predicted CD8+ T cell epitope density (1.5 per residue) among SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
source: For CD8+ T cells, the lowest predicted epitope density occurs in ORF3d (1.5 per residue), which is unexpected given its own amino acid content (p=0.150) and compared to short unannotated ORFs (p=0.078; permutation tests).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction of T cell epitopes using NetMHCpan.

claim: ORF3d, N, and ORF8 have the lowest predicted CD8+ T cell epitope densities and also elicit the strongest antibody responses in COVID-19 patient sera.
source: The next lowest densities occur in N and ORF8 (Figure 3A). Intriguingly, as previously mentioned, these three peptides (ORF3d, N, and ORF8) also elicit the strongest antibody (B cell epitope) responses measured in COVID-19 patient sera (Hachim et al., 2020), suggesting a possible balance between CD8+ T and B cell epitopes.
evidence: This is based on computational epitope prediction and citation to antibody response data, with inference about immune balance.

claim: The shorter ORF3d-2 isoform contains zero predicted CD8+ T cell epitopes, which is a highly significant depletion.
source: Focusing instead on the shorter ORF3d-2 isoform, this protein contains zero predicted epitopes, which is a highly significant depletion given its own amino acid content (p=0.001) and compared to short unannotated ORFs (p=0.001).
evidence: This is based on computational epitope prediction and statistical testing.

claim: ORF3c has the highest predicted CD8+ T cell epitope density (8.4 per residue).
source: In stark contrast to ORF3d, ORF3c has the highest predicted CD8+ T cell epitope density (8.4 per residue), apparently as a function of its amino acid content (i.e. not differing from its randomized peptides; p=0.996).
evidence: This is based on computational epitope prediction.

claim: The maximum correlation between hydrophobicity profiles occurs between the frames of ORF3a (ss11) and ORF3d (ss12) in the region encoding ORF3d, with rS = 0.87 (p=5.79 × 10−13).
source: The maximum correlation observed occurs between the frames of ORF3a (ss11) and ORF3d (ss12) in the region encoding ORF3d (ORF3a residues 64–102), with rS = 0.87 (p=5.79 × 10−13, Spearman's rank), which is much stronger than the correlation between these frames observed for the non-OLG residues of ORF3a (rS = 0.27, p=8.70 × 10−4) (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of hydrophobicity profiles.

claim: The conservation of a structure-related property with the ORF3a protein provides further evidence for ORF3d functionality.
source: This conservation of a structure-related property with the ORF3a protein provides further evidence for ORF3d functionality, and may predispose this region toward de novo gene birth.
evidence: This is inferred from the hydrophobicity correlation analysis.

claim: ORF3d is intact in only two sequences: SARS-CoV-2 Wuhan-Hu-1 and pangolin-CoVs from Guangxi (GX/P5L).
source: Specifically, ORF3d is intact in only two sequences: SARS-CoV-2 Wuhan-Hu-1 and pangolin-CoVs from Guangxi (GX/P5L).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis across 21 coronavirus genomes.

claim: Full-length ORF3b is intact in only three sequences: SARS-CoV TW11, SARS-CoV Tor2, and bat-CoV Rs7327.
source: Full-length ORF3b is intact in only three sequences: SARS-CoV TW11, SARS-CoV Tor2, and bat-CoV Rs7327, with the remainder having premature STOP codons (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The taxonomic distribution of ORF3d is incongruent with whole-genome phylogenies.
source: However, the taxonomic distribution of this ORF is incongruent with whole-genome phylogenies in that ORF3d is intact in the pangolin-CoV more distantly related to SARS-CoV-2 (GX/P5L) but not the more closely related one (GD/1) (Figure 4), a finding confirmed by the alignment of Boni et al., 2020.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and comparison to sequence alignments.

claim: ORF3d contains STOP codons in the closely related bat-CoV RmYN02.
source: New sequence data reveal similarly puzzling trends: ORF3d contains STOP codons in the closely related bat-CoV RmYN02 (GISAID: EPI_ISL_412977; data not shown), but it is intact in three more distantly related bat-CoVs discovered in Rwanda and Uganda, where it is further extended by 20 codons (total 78 codons) but shows no evidence of conservation with SARS-CoV-2 (Wells et al., 2020 and pers. comm; data not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of new sequence data.

claim: Phylogenies of the 21 Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus genomes built on ORF3a are incongruent with whole-genome phylogenies, likely due to recombination breakpoints in ORF3a near ORF3d.
source: Further, phylogenies of the 21 Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus genomes built on ORF3a are incongruent with whole-genome phylogenies, likely due to the presence of recombination breakpoints in ORF3a near ORF3d (Boni et al., 2020; Rehman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and citations to studies identifying recombination.

claim: The only gene to show significant evidence of purifying selection at all three evolutionary levels is the nucleocapsid gene N.
source: The only gene to show significant evidence of purifying selection at all three evolutionary levels is the nucleocapsid gene N (Figure 5), which undergoes disproportionately low rates of nonsynonymous change (dN/dS < 1 and πN/πS < 1) specifically in its non-OLG regions, evidencing strict functional constraint.
evidence: This is based on dN/dS analysis at three evolutionary levels.

claim: N is the most highly expressed gene.
source: N is also the most highly expressed gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), confirming that selection has more opportunity to act when a protein is manufactured in abundance (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1) (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry and ribosome profiling data.

claim: Comparison of Wuhan-Hu-1 to pangolin-CoV GX/P5L yields OLG dN/dS = 0.14 (p=0.264) for ORF3d.
source: With respect to ORF3d, comparison of Wuhan-Hu-1 to pangolin-CoV GX/P5L (NCBI: MT040335.1) yields OLG dN/dS = 0.14 (p=0.264) (Figure 5), whereas inclusion of a third allele found in pangolin-CoV GX/P4L (NCBI: MT040333.1) yields 0.43 (p=0.488) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on OLGenie analysis of sequence divergence.

claim: Pairwise comparisons of each sequence to SARS-CoV-2 reveal OLG dN/dS < 1 that is specific to the reading frame, genome positions, and species in which ORF3d is intact (pangolin-CoV GX/P5L).
source: Pairwise comparisons of each sequence to SARS-CoV-2 reveal OLG dN/dS < 1 that is specific to the reading frame, genome positions, and species in which ORF3d is intact (pangolin-CoV GX/P5L) (Figure 6, left).
evidence: This is based on sliding window analysis of selection across coronavirus genomes.

claim: One high-frequency mutation occurred in ORF3d: G25563U, denoted ORF3d-LOF (ORF3d-loss-of-function).
source: One high-frequency mutation occurred in ORF3d: G25563U, here denoted ORF3d-LOF (ORF3d-loss-of-function).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SARS-CoV-2 consensus sequences from GISAID.

claim: G25563U causes a STOP codon in ORF3d (ORF3d-E14*) but nonsynonymous changes in both ORF3a (ORF3a-Q57H) and ORF3c (ORF3c-R36I).
source: This mutation causes a STOP codon in ORF3d (ORF3d-E14*) but nonsynonymous changes in both ORF3a (ORF3a-Q57H) and ORF3c (ORF3c-R36I), another OLG that overlaps this site (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of the mutation's effects on overlapping genes.

claim: ORF3d-LOF is not observed in any other species member included in the analysis.
source: ORF3d-LOF is not observed in any other species member included in our analysis (Figure 4; SARS-related-CoV_ALN.fasta, supplementary data).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: During the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic, ORF3d-LOF increased in frequency in multiple locations.
source: During the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic, ORF3d-LOF increased in frequency (Supplementary file 1) in multiple locations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 1), making this mutation a candidate for natural selection on ORF3a, ORF3c, ORF3d, or any combination thereof (Kosakovsky-Pond, 2020).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of allele frequencies across locations.

claim: The EP haplotype is first detected in German patient #4 and is a documented founder for coronavirus spread in Germany.
source: The EP haplotype is first detected in German patient #4 and is a documented founder for coronavirus spread in Germany (Rothe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rothe et al., 2020 documenting the German outbreak.

claim: Despite its expected predominance in Europe due to a founder effect, the EP haplotype is extremely rare.
source: Surprisingly, despite its expected predominance in Europe due to a founder effect, the EP haplotype is extremely rare.
evidence: This is based on analysis of haplotype frequencies in GISAID data.

claim: Haplotypes with one additional mutation (C14408U; RdRp-P323L) on the EP background are common in Europe.
source: By contrast, haplotypes with one additional mutation (C14408U; RdRp-P323L) on the EP background are common in Europe, and ORF3d-LOF occurred very early on this background to create EP+1+LOF from EP+1.
evidence: This is based on analysis of haplotype frequencies and mutational paths.

claim: ORF3d does not show significant evidence of selection at the within-host level, with OLG πN/πS = 1.5 (p=0.584).
source: Using these variants to estimate within-host diversity, ORF3d does not show significant evidence of selection, with OLG πN/πS = 1.5 (p=0.584) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on analysis of within-host SNPs from deeply sequenced samples.

claim: ORF3d-LOF is observed as a minor allele in three (0.94%) of 320 within-host samples.
source: For ORF3d, we observe ORF3d-LOF as a minor allele in three (0.94%) of 320 samples (frequencies of 20.7%, 6.0%, and 2.2% in samples SRR11410536, SRR11479046, and SRR11494643, respectively).
evidence: This is based on analysis of within-host variant data.

claim: A STOP mutation (A404U; NSP1-L47*) is never a major allele but is observed at low frequencies in 44% of samples.
source: Surprisingly, another STOP mutation (A404U; NSP1-L47*) is never a major allele but is observed at low frequencies in 44% of samples (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), unexplainable by mutational bias and warranting investigation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of recurrent mutations across within-host samples.

claim: The annotation of a newly emerged virus is difficult, particularly in genome regions subject to frequent gene gain and loss.
source: The annotation of a newly emerged virus is difficult, particularly in genome regions subject to frequent gene gain and loss.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about challenges in viral genome annotation.

claim: De novo and homology-based annotation are both essential, followed by careful expression analyses using multi-omic data and evolutionary analyses within and between species.
source: Therefore, de novo and homology-based annotation are both essential, followed by careful expression analyses using multi-omic data and evolutionary analyses within and between species.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the study's approach.

claim: Homology between ORF3b (SARS-CoV) and ORF3d (SARS-CoV-2) has erroneously been implied, leading to unwarranted inferences of shared functionality.
source: For example, homology between ORF3b (SARS-CoV) and ORF3d (SARS-CoV-2) has erroneously been implied, leading to unwarranted inferences of shared functionality (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of misannotations in the literature.

claim: The absence of full-length ORF3b in SARS-CoV-2 may be immunologically important.
source: Thus, the absence or truncation of ORF3b in SARS-CoV-2 may be immunologically important (Yuen et al., 2020), for example in the suppression of type I interferon induction (Konno et al., 2020; Lokugamage et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citations to studies on ORF3b function and speculation about immunological consequences.

claim: The apparent presence of ORF3d coincident with the inferred entry of SARS-CoV-2 into humans suggests that this gene is functionally relevant for the emergent properties of SARS-CoV-2.
source: With respect to gene gain, the apparent presence of ORF3d coincident with the inferred entry of SARS-CoV-2 into humans from a hitherto undetermined reservoir host suggests that this gene is functionally relevant for the emergent properties of SARS-CoV-2, analogous to asp for HIV-1-M (Cassan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the taxonomic distribution of ORF3d and comparison to HIV-1, with speculation about functional relevance.

claim: Failure to account for OLGs can lead to erroneous inference of (or failure to detect) natural selection in known genes.
source: Failure to account for OLGs can lead to erroneous inference of (or failure to detect) natural selection in known genes, and vice versa.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about the effects of overlapping reading frames on selection analysis.

claim: A synonymous variant in one reading frame is very likely to be nonsynonymous in a second overlapping frame.
source: For example, a synonymous variant in one reading frame is very likely to be nonsynonymous in a second overlapping frame.
evidence: This is based on knowledge about the genetic code and overlapping genes.

claim: Purifying selection in the second frame usually lowers dS (raises dN/dS) in the first frame, increasing the likelihood of mis-inferring positive selection.
source: As a result, purifying selection in the second frame usually lowers dS (raises dN/dS) in the first frame, increasing the likelihood of mis-inferring positive selection (Holmes et al., 2006; Sabath et al., 2008; Nelson et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on selection analysis in overlapping genes.

claim: ORF3d-2 shows evidence of higher overall expression than ORF3d.
source: ORF3d-2, a shorter isoform of ORF3d (Table 1), shows evidence of higher overall expression than ORF3d (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data.

claim: ORF3c shows deep conservation among viruses of this species.
source: Although not evolutionarily novel, the recently discovered ORF3c (Table 1) shows deep conservation among viruses of this species (Cagliani et al., 2020; Firth, 2020; Jungreis et al., 2020), the lowest πN/πS ratio observed in our between-host analysis (Figure 5), strong evidence for translation in SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 2), and the highest predicted CD8+ T cell epitope density (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis, selection analysis, ribosome profiling, and epitope prediction.

claim: S-iORF2 shows evidence of translation from ribosome profiling and between-host comparisons suggest purifying selection (πN/πS = 0.22, p=0.0278).
source: Within S, S-iORF2 (genome positions 21768–21863) also shows evidence of translation from ribosome profiling (Finkel et al., 2020), and between-host comparisons suggest purifying selection (πN/πS = 0.22, p=0.0278) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on ribosome profiling data and selection analysis.

claim: Many genes in SARS-CoV-2 are under relaxed purifying selection, consistent with the exponential growth of the virus.
source: Our comprehensive evolutionary analysis of the SARS-CoV-2 genome demonstrates that many genes are under relaxed purifying selection, consistent with the exponential growth of the virus (Gazave et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on selection analysis and citation to theory about selection during population expansion.

claim: At the between-host level, nucleotide diversity increases somewhat over the initial period of the COVID-19 pandemic, tracking the number of locations sampled, while the πN/πS ratio remains relatively constant at 0.46 (±0.030 SEM).
source: At the between-host level, nucleotide diversity increases somewhat over the initial period of the COVID-19 pandemic, tracking the number of locations sampled, while the πN/πS ratio remains relatively constant at 0.46 (±0.030 SEM) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of diversity in GISAID sequences.

claim: ORF3d and ORF8 are among the youngest genes in SARS-CoV-2, being taxonomically restricted to a subset of betacoronaviruses.
source: ORF3d and ORF8 are among the youngest genes in SARS-CoV-2, being taxonomically restricted to a subset of betacoronaviruses (Cui et al., 2019), and both exhibit high rates of change and turnover (Figure 1; Figure 5; SARS-related-CoV_ALN.fasta, supplementary data).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis and citation to previous work.

claim: ORF3d and ORF8 both exhibit strong antibody (B cell epitope) responses and predicted T cell epitope depletion in SARS-CoV-2.
source: However, ORF3d and ORF8 both exhibit strong antibody (B cell epitope) responses (Hachim et al., 2020) and predicted T cell epitope depletion (Figure 3) in SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is based on citation to antibody response data and computational epitope prediction.

claim: The loss or truncation of ORF3d and ORF8 may share an immunological basis.
source: Thus, the loss or truncation of these genes may share an immunological basis and deserves further attention.
evidence: This is speculation based on the immunological properties of these genes.

claim: The slower 'spread' of EP–3 and EP may be an artifact of a sampling policy bias in case isolation.
source: First, the slower 'spread' of EP–3 and EP may be an artifact of a sampling policy bias in case isolation: testing and quarantine were preferentially applied to travellers who had recently visited Wuhan, which may have led to selective detection, isolation, and tracing of these haplotypes rather than those with mutations occurring within Europe (e.g. C14408U and G25563U).
evidence: This is speculation about potential sampling biases.

claim: It is possible that the EP haplotype was effectively controlled, while EP+1 was introduced independently.
source: Second, it is possible that the EP haplotype was effectively controlled, while EP+1 was introduced independently (Worobey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Worobey et al., 2020.

claim: The spread of G25563U seems to be linked with RdRp-P323L and Spike-D614G, a variant with predicted functional relevance.
source: Third, although G25563U itself simultaneously causes ORF3a-Q57H, ORF3c-R36I, and ORF3d-E14* (ORF3d-LOF), its spread seems to be linked with RdRp-P323L and Spike-D614G, a variant with predicted functional relevance (e.g. see Korber et al., 2020; Plante et al., 2020; Yurkovetskiy et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on haplotype analysis and citations to studies on Spike-D614G.

claim: It is possible that G25563U is neutral while a linked variant(s) is under selection.
source: Thus, it is possible that G25563U is neutral while a linked variant(s) is under selection.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary dynamics of linked mutations.

claim: ORF3d may be expressed at low levels.
source: This may be due to several reasons: (1) ORF3d may be expressed at low levels;
evidence: This is speculation about why ORF3d was not detected by mass spectrometry.

claim: ORF3d is short, and tryptic digestion of ORF3d generates only two peptides potentially detectable by MS.
source: (2) ORF3d is short, and tryptic digestion of ORF3d generates only two peptides potentially detectable by MS;
evidence: This is based on knowledge about mass spectrometry limitations for short proteins.

claim: The tryptic peptides derived from ORF3d may not be amenable to detection by MS even under the best possible conditions.
source: (3) the tryptic peptides derived from ORF3d may not be amenable to detection by MS even under the best possible conditions, as suggested by its relatively low MS intensity even in an overexpression experiment ('ORF3b' in Gordon et al., 2020);
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2020 showing low MS intensity.

claim: Hitherto unknown post-translational modifications of ORF3d could prohibit detection by mass spectrometry.
source: and (4) hitherto unknown post-translational modifications of ORF3d could prohibit detection.
evidence: This is speculation about potential post-translational modifications.
